en: Firing guns and drawing bows,
Fighting where we stand, without fleeing,
Driving your migrating train across the ford,
With companions in good number,
From the clamorous Kalmyks
Then take your revenge.
I followed the handed-down accounts,
I asked those who knew:
Khan Koshoy, khan of the Katagan,
Is an elder in the likeness of a prophet,
A saint born greater than other men;
His blessing enriched a warrior,
His prayer brought light to a soul.
Those who saw his majesty took fright;
Having become a disciple of twelve spiritual guides,
Your elder Koshoy, that worthy hero,
Studied five years in Mecca;
He received a letter from the caliph.
Through this, that Koshoy
Was called Koshoy the Wise.
In Egypt and Baghdad
He studied five more years.
That is the renowned hero Koshoy;
He is a lion to bind about your waist as support.
He wore a broad, old, grimy sheepskin coat,
He rode a bay leopard of a horse;
If a thousand tümen troops set out,
He charged them with a battle cry.
His valor is distinct, his wrath is mighty;
Your heroic elder Koshoy is there.
The market that was shut and bound—
Hero Koshoy opened its fortune;
The champion held in confinement—
Hero Koshoy freed his hands.
When, in days past, Aykozho's Bilerik
Was captured by the Chinese,
To their pit forty ropes in height
They took him and cast him in,
My elder Koshoy, that worthy hero,
Until the pliant weed stems ripened,
Until the autumn gossamer flew,
Fought hard for six full months.
Girding his waist with a jekene belt,
Against seven tümen Chinese
He went alone into their midst and attacked,
Putting on iron armor,
Into the seething Chinese
My elder Khan Koshoy plunged.
He slaughtered much of that people, they say;
He wrought an extraordinary slaughter, they say.
Aykozho's Bilerik
He wrested from the Chinese, they say.
At Chech-Töbö in At-Bashy
He made his home, they say.
From Alty-Shaar and Margalang
He exacted tribute firmly, they say.
That precious land of Zheti-Özön
He skillfully made his country;
The lost and scattered Kyrgyz
He managed to make into a people.
He raised a harrier into a hunting hawk,
Gathered disparate folk into a nation,
Raised a stray bird into a hunting hawk,
Gathered wandering people into a nation.
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan
Built his fortress of stone, they say.
To those lost and scattered people,
My elder, old Koshoy,
Became a leader, they say.
He is the hero to hold fast to;
He is the learned lion Koshoy.
My elder, old Koshoy,
Is a saintly scion, an outstanding khan;
His bravery is of another kind,
His wolf-maned valor plain to see.
His wide-set eyes are like the morning star,
His moonlike ears are like shields,
His eyes are like the beds of lakes,
As if to suck in whatever they meet.
He is support to bind about your waist,
He is a hero greater than other mortals.
My child, Manas, hear this well:
Those are the words Akbaltay has spoken.
When we were driven away,
When we reached this Altai,
When many years had passed,
I asked again and heard these words:
Dwelling in Eki-Kemin,
Tethering twin black horses,
Sowing his rice as an autumn crop,
To his swift horse, from the rice,
Feeding its barnyard grass as he tethered it,
Honing his black tongue,
Speaking eloquently before the khan,
Making the dark forest his livestock,
Making a dark cave his home,
From being alone, growing numerous,
From being poor, growing rich,
Hero Ürbü, whose father was Taz,
He too arose a hero from the Kyrgyz;
I heard he had found a place to settle.
There is support to bind about your waist;
He too is a hero who will be your companion.
Let us not turn the steed's head aside;
Let us not stay in this Altai.
This Altai is no land for us;
These Chinese are no people for us.”
Akbaltay speaks words of every kind.
Hearing the words of Akbaltay,
Hearing that his rallying cry was “Kyrgyz,”
The forty boys he led along,
Their auspicious one was Kutubiy.
“Let me find my many lands;
Let me too take him as a companion.
If these words of yours are true,
Let me go to Koshoy Khan.”
Surging like a hawk,
Mounting Toruchaar and making ready,
Surging like a lion,
Lion Manas, the wolf-maned hero,
Mounted and set out toward the Kyrgyz, fully prepared.
The forty boys he led along
Raced across the rolling hills,
Crossed ridge after swelling ridge,
Crossed a striking dark upland,
Skirted another mountain.
Your wolf-maned Manas traveled on,
Traveled far, not sparing his horse,
Traveled many roads without wearying.
A sable hat upon his head,
The fearless one called a lion
Saw lovely lands and lovely lakes,
Forded a broad, long-flowing river,
And along Kyyaz and Tekes
He made his way now.
Was it not the finest of lands?
Would not a settler prosper there?
There was snow upon its mountains,
There were rooks in its forest;
Of every kind of living creature,
All the animals were there.
There were hares in its hollows,
There were snakes in its depressions,
There were ibex on its terraces,
There were deer on its knolls,
There were argali on its hills,
There were foxes on its plains,
There were wild asses on its steppes.
Its lizards were like snakes,
Its wild asses like two-year-old colts;
If you looked upon its snakes,
They were like ropes six fathoms long.
Allah Most High, in His might,
Had created creatures of every kind.
Nightingales sang in a clamor;
When they sang their twisting trills,
A grieving person could not bear to hear.
Many a soul, sobbing aloud,
Could not leave that spot.
Cuckoos called upon its mountains,
Parrots made music in its willows;
The birds that hatched in birches
Were preparing for their flight;
The birds that hatched in poplars
Were urging themselves into flight.
Was it not the finest of lands?
Would not a settler prosper there!
The tops of its willows bent;
Such were its wondrous sights—
The surface of its sand was traced with lines,
Its saplings were like plane trees,
Its little birds like snowcocks.
Was it not the best of lands?
Would not a mortal dwelling there prosper!
Rejoicing at this sight,
Crossing stark, jutting mountains,
Passing many deep ravines,
Crossing passes, treading stones,
Lion Manas took the road.
When did your hero ever spare himself?
To the hollow of Ükürchü,
Along Üch-Kapkak,
Wolf-maned Manas drew near.
To the ridge of Bel-Moynok
Your wolf-maned one headed out,
Toward the land of Üch-Karkyra.
Its fescue and meadow grasses
Had grown waist-high and rotted,
Its zhyltyrkan grass and wormwood.
Was this a land where people
Could fail to camp in plenty for the summer?
Its leaves were like hides;
There lay Karkyra,
Its black insects as big as thumbs,
Its hogweed as thick as forearms.
When its maral deer took fright and bolted,
They were like pale, white-blazed cows.
Rejoicing at this sight,
Seemingly surveying the land,
Your consummate falcon Manas
Traveled through Üch-Karkyra, they say.
Kyzyl-Kyya, a precious road;
Hero Manas, whom Kydyr had visited,
Excited by the wondrous sight,
Flashed over the pass and descended,
And came upon Issyk-Kul.
It was abundance, it was support,
A land for mortals to behold,
A land that made the man
Who settled there a khan.
All those along its shores
It was a land to make them rich.
In its midst was a deep-blue lake;
Its waters held a thousand places of honor.
The people dwelling there would grow rich;
There was good fortune in its lake!
At a little hill like a gray ridge,
Manas dismounted and dug the earth.
It was a land of sacred power:
Turning up two fingerbreadths of soil,
There was inexhaustible gold.
My dear Issyk-Kul,
Was it not the finest of lands?
Would not a dweller prosper there?
There could be no land so wondrous,
There could be no lake so wondrous!
It was a ridge of knoll upon knoll,
A land bearing rugged passes.
Its knolls came curving round,
From the knolls the deer poured down;
There lay the creatures,
The grasses on the knolls thinned out;
From the hills the argali poured down,
The grasses on the hills thinned out.
From every gully, roaring,
Springs poured forth by the thousand.
On this side and that, the land was narrow,
And in its midst, shining,
There was a lovely deep-blue lake.
Countless troops could not fit on its land;
The spearheads would clash,
People's heads would knock together—
It was a place that would cause trouble.
“My adversary is Kakanchyn;
The Chinese I must fight are mighty.
If they attack from every side,
Every river valley is a road.”
He traveled down along Issyk-Kul,
Traveled far, not sparing his horse,
Thinking many thoughts as he pondered.
Where he camped, your wolf-maned one
Laid out ordo and played games.
Finding no land that drew his gaze,
To take as shelter over him,
Your wolf-maned Manas found no people.
Finding no place to pitch camp in full strength,
